query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles is governed by the formation of localized short‐range chemical ordering that, together with the resulting internal lattice strain from heterogeneous metal–metal bond energies, kinetically stabilizes regions of the particle. This stabilization delays surface premelting and sharpens the overall melting transition relative to a perfectly random solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles with an overall random (but slightly short-range ordered) atomic distribution.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating experiments at a constant ramp rate across the premelting to melting temperature regime.
generation.conditions: Under an inert atmosphere with identical particle sizes (~10–20 nm) and composition, ensuring that the only variable is the degree of local chemical ordering. Temperature is ramped at a constant rate to mitigate kinetic artifacts.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic configurations (short‐range order) and the associated internal lattice strain arising from heterogeneous bonding.
generation.mechanism: Because the five constituent metals have different bond strengths and mixing enthalpies, some regions within the nanoparticle form more favorable heteroatomic clusters. These clusters create elastic strain fields that hinder surface atom migration until higher local temperatures, thereby shifting the onset of premelting and sharpening the melting transition (as nucleation of the liquid phase becomes more cooperative).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to nanoparticles with a near-ideal random atomic distribution, nanoparticles showing enhanced local ordering (as detected by advanced STEM-EDX and NMF methods) will exhibit a higher premelting onset temperature and a steeper melting transition due to the kinetic stabilization provided by the local strain fields.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized to minimize short-range ordering so that the elemental distribution closely approaches a random, statistically homogeneous state.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for HEA nanoparticles of similar size (~10–20 nm) and equimolar composition, under inert atmosphere conditions and with controlled heating rates where kinetic processing effects (e.g., limited diffusion) are comparable. It might not apply if significant surface segregation or drastic compositional changes occur due to evaporation or other high-temperature phenomena.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantification of the contributions from bond heterogeneity and strain to the shift in melting behavior remains uncertain. There is also uncertainty in isolating the effects of short-range ordering from potential surface segregation phenomena during heating.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles under conditions designed to yield varying degrees of short-range chemical ordering (e.g., by adjusting cooling rates after synthesis). Subject all samples to identical controlled heating experiments with a constant ramp rate while monitoring in situ the onset of surface premelting and complete melting via high-resolution TEM and diffraction techniques. Concurrently, use STEM-EDX and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to quantify the degree of short-range ordering and X-ray diffraction to assess internal lattice strain for each sample.
measurements: Premelting onset temperature (e.g., via in situ TEM or DSC)
Quantification of local chemical ordering (using STEM-EDX/NMF)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with enhanced short-range ordering and associated strain do not reproducibly exhibit a higher premelting onset temperature or steeper melting transition compared to more random nanoparticles, or if no correlation is found between the degree of local ordering and changes in the thermal transition kinetics, the hypothesis must be rejected.

The atomic structure of the individual HEA particles is also investigated by scanning transmission electron microscopy combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (STEM-EDX). Based on the elemental distribution maps created from STEM-EDX measurements for the fcc-phase HEA, shown in Fig. 3c, the spatial distribution of all elements within this one particulate appears completely and equally mixed. However, upon more detailed analysis, i.e., by using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), there appears to be some segregation of different elements in various areas. The area highlighted in red in Fig. 3d shows the most dominant NMF loading, which contains all five elements. This indicates that a major fraction of the particle shows complete mixing between the five elements. The green loading, however, highlights areas containing all elements except for Pt. All the resulting structures show random distribution of the five elements, and no apparent chemical ordering such as the segregation of single elements or formation of intermetallic phases was observed, confirming the formation of HEA under the given conditions. This finding is further corroborated by statistical analysis of the averaged composition of the nearest-neighbor lattice sites (with a cutoff radius of 3.0 Å) for a given element (Fig. 8d–i). For an ideal solid solution, this averaged composition should be equal to the nominal composition of the HEA nanoparticle, which are represented by the dash lines in Fig. 8d–i. Our results show that the nearest-neighbor (NN) compositions averaged over all the atoms only deviate slightly from the nominal composition throughout the three temperatures investigated, implying the absence of long-range chemical ordering. On the other hand, some degree of short-range ordering is predicted in the modeled nanoparticle: Fe, Co, and Ni atoms exhibit a relatively higher affinity around Mo atom, whereas there is a moderate repulsive interaction between Cu-Mo, Fe-Co, Co-Ni, and Co-Cu atom pairs.
